title: Introduction to Securities Broking Operations
big_picture: Every trade is a relay race run by three teams inside the broker. The front office signs up the client (KYC, account kit, UCC) and gets the order onto the exchange; the middle office checks every order against limits and margins, because if the client defaults the broker pays; the back office enriches and allocates the trade, issues the contract note, settles on T+1 and keeps the books for 8 years. Around the race sit the rules of the track: order types and matching, session timings, taxes and fees, and the IT, BCP and cyber-security safety nets.
exam_focus: Contract note: within 24 hours, ECN rules, contents; statutory charges (STT, GST, stamp duty) vs regulatory levies (SEBI fees, exchange charges)
On-boarding: six kit documents, SARAL AOF, PAN exemptions, IPV/VIPV, KRA vs CKYCR (10 days), UCC, copy of documents in 7 days, PoA vs DDPI
Orders: market/limit/stop loss, which conditions are unavailable (GTC, GTD, AON, MF), price-time priority at passive price, call auction equilibrium
Numbers: brokerage caps (2.5%, 25 paise, ₹100 per lot), trade annulment (30/60 min, 5%, ₹1-10 lakh), bulk 0.5% vs block ₹25 crore, SEBI fee 10/5/2
Session timings: block windows 8:45-9:00 and 2:05-2:20, pre-open 9:00-9:15, normal 9:15-3:30, post-close 3:40-4:00, call auction and special pre-open
Resilience: glitch rules (5 min, 2 hours, T+1, 14 days, 10,000 clients), NSE-BSE backup (75/15 min), CSCRF goals and categories, IRRA replaced by Contingency Pool Trading (new)
Middle and back office: types of risk, client code modification, books under SC(R)R 1957 kept 8 years, T+1 timeline

blocks.text: A trade is the conversion of an order placed on the exchange into a pay-in and pay-out of funds and securities. It is not finished when it matches; it ends only when it is settled. Along the way it passes investors, brokers, exchanges, the clearing corporation, clearing banks, DPs and custodians, in five steps:

items.text: By the investor/client or broker.

items.title: Risk management and order routing
items.text: Broker's RMS checks the order and routes it through the trading platform.

items.title: Matching and conversion into trade
items.text: Exchange matches it with a counter order.

items.title: Confirmation of trades
items.text: To broker and client; for institutions, affirmed by the custodian.

items.title: Clearing and settlement
items.text: Obligations worked out; funds and securities change hands.

blocks.text: Restaurant picture: the waiter takes and sends the order (front), the manager checks you can pay (middle), the cashier/accountant bills you and keeps the books (back).
Order routing is front office, but the risk management on that order is middle office. Confirmation is back office.

sections.title: Placing Orders: TWS, Phone, Internet, DMA and Algos

blocks.text: The Trader Workstation (TWS) is the terminal through which a member enters orders into the exchange's trading system. Each trader logs in with a unique Trading Member ID and User ID, for trading or enquiry.

Members may also build customised workstations and connect via CTCL (Computer to Computer Link), IBT (Internet Based Trading), DMA, STWT (Securities Trading through Wireless Technology), ALGO and SOR (Smart Order Router), over leased line, VSAT or co-location (broker/vendor systems placed in or near the exchange premises on a direct private network).

Order evidence. A broker may execute a client's trade only after keeping evidence that the client placed the order: a physical record signed by the client, telephone recording, e-mail from the authorised e-mail ID, internet transaction log, SMS record, or any other legally verifiable record. In a dispute the broker must produce it; if it can't (e.g. technical failure), it must justify why, and evidence such as the client's post-trade confirmation or payment/delivery for that trade may be considered.

head: Situation
Keep order evidence for
rows: Period for which arbitration accepts complaints, currently 3 years

blocks.text: Phone orders: the client calls numbers notified by the broker; a Dealing Desk Executive verifies him with questions including user ID and TPIN. Telephone recording of client instructions is mandatory (SEBI, March 22, 2018). Internet trading and wireless trading (on the WAP platform) need the broker to get permission from the stock exchange and meet SEBI's minimum conditions.

Direct Market Access (DMA) gives clients direct access to the exchange through the broker's infrastructure, without manual intervention by the broker. SEBI introduced it in 2008 for institutional investors. Benefits: client control over orders, faster execution, fewer manual errors, transparency, liquidity, lower impact cost on large orders, better audit trails, and better hedging/arbitrage using algos. It may be used by the client or its investment manager (a SEBI-registered entity, who signs the documents); the exchange may specify which categories of investors can get DMA; the broker needs exchange permission and must authorise each user after KYC and due diligence.

Algorithmic trading: any order generated using automated execution logic. Automated trading: software that generates and pushes orders into the exchange system automatically once set parameters are met. HFT is latency-sensitive algo trading with high daily portfolio turnover and a high order-to-trade ratio (OTR).
Retail algos via APIs (SEBI, February 04, 2025): the broker is the principal and the algo provider/fintech is the broker's agent.

items: Home-made retail algos must be registered with the exchange (through the broker) only above the orders-per-second (OPS) threshold; brokers must flag all orders above it as algo orders.
Algo providers are not directly regulated by SEBI but must be empanelled with exchanges.
All algo orders go through broker servers located in India, with minimum checks: price, quantity limit, order value.
Algo trading needs the exchange's prior permission; exchanges must give fair, equitable access to co-location.
Algo systems face a system audit every six months by a certified system auditor.

blocks.text: Whatever the channel, the broker confirms the order with the client and enters it; the exchange confirms every order it receives and time-stamps it. The conditions attached (market, limit, etc.) tell the exchange how to execute it.
Retail algo rule in one line: broker = principal, algo provider = agent. Like a driving school: the school holds the licence and the liability; the instructor works under it.

DMA was for institutional clients, not retail. Algo audit is every six months, not yearly. Algo providers are empanelled with exchanges, not SEBI-registered. A home-made retail algo needs registration only above the OPS threshold.

An efficient risk management system is integral to an efficient settlement system: it measures and manages the firm's exposure to the risks central to its business. Strong internal risk controls protect:

items: The firm, against market, credit, liquidity, operational and legal risks
The financial industry, against systemic risk
The firm's customers, against large non-market losses (firm failure, misappropriation, fraud)
The firm and its franchise, against reputational risk

blocks.text: The broker must run an online RMS with upfront real-time checks on every order, with pre-defined limits such as order quantity and value, symbol-wise user order/quantity, user/branch order and order price. Only orders within the RMS parameters reach the exchange's trading engine.
Brokers collect upfront margin before execution, so the RMS lets through only orders backed by sufficient margin.

sections.title: Order Matching, Trade Confirmation and the Contract Note (Box 3.1)

blocks.text: Orders match on price-time priority: best price first (best buy = highest bid, best sell = lowest offer), then earliest time. On a match the exchange sends a trade confirmation to the broker, who informs the client by messages and the contract note. Unexecuted orders can be modified/cancelled in trading hours; a trade can be cancelled only by mutual consent, with exchange approval under the trade annulment policy (usually for order entry errors).
Matching rule: price first, then the clock. Order size never jumps the queue.

Contract note: the legal record of a transaction done on an exchange through a broker. It confirms the day's trades for the client and creates a legally enforceable relationship between broker and client for their settlement. Every client trade needs one, in the exchange's format.
Issue it within 24 hours of execution, physical or electronic as the client chooses.

blocks.text: A contract note is not the agreement signed before trading or a margin note; it confirms trades of a particular day. STT, GST, stamp duty are statutory; SEBI fees and exchange charges are regulatory levies.

sections.title: Institutional Trades: Custodian Affirmation and STP

blocks.text: Institutions (mutual funds, FPIs, insurers) settle cash-segment trades through custodians, who are clearing members of the exchange. Why? The institution wants a specialist that settles on its behalf and backs the trade with the institution's collateral.

items.title: CP code at order entry
items.text: The broker tags the trade with the custodian's custodian participant (CP) code.

items.title: Custodian checks
items.text: Security details, side of trade, price range etc., as specified by the institutional client.

items.title: Custodian confirms
items.text: It confirms (affirms) whether it will settle the trade.

items.title: Obligation moves
items.text: The clearing corporation assigns the settlement obligation to the custodian.

items.title: Risk monitored
items.text: The custodian keeps measuring its risk against the collateral the institution has submitted.

blocks.text: Since 2004, SEBI requires all institutional trades to go through Straight Through Processing (STP): one system captures and processes the trade electronically in one pass, from first 'deal' to final settlement, across front, middle and back office. No manual re-entry, faster and cheaper settlement, fewer errors, shorter clearing time, and a flexible infrastructure for online processing.
STP: one-pass electronic processing from deal to settlement, mandatory for institutional trades since 2004.

The exchange sends trades to the clearing corporation (CC). After custodian/clearing member affirmation, the CC applies multilateral netting to fix obligations. It settles through clearing banks (funds) and depositories (securities), linking the two. Members must deliver funds/securities before pay-in time; the CC then pays out.
SEBI's circular of March 21, 2024 introduced an optional T+0 settlement in equity cash, alongside T+1.

The front office does order capture and execution and owns the client relationship. Dealers and sales staff sit here; dealers are 'the face of the broker'. The sales force pitches trading ideas, takes orders, passes them to the trading desk and brings in new clients.

Advertisements must not breach the Code of Conduct under the Stock Brokers Regulations, 2026 or exchange bye-laws (this covers websites, subsidiaries and group companies too). Every advertisement needs the prior approval of the stock exchange and must follow the exchange's Code for Advertisements.
Advertisement approval: stock exchange, not SEBI or the depository.

blocks.text: SEBI requires the standard documents to be given in electronic or physical form, as the client prefers (asked in the form); if electronic, the broker keeps logs. The Account Opening Form has two parts: Part I, the KYC form (CERSAI's template, used by all intermediaries for individuals and legal entities) and Part II, additional information for trading (bank and demat details, trading preferences, past actions, nomination).

Six-pack kit: Form, Rights, Risks, Guide, Policies, Price list.

SARAL AOF: a simplified form for new individual investors in the cash segment who do not use internet trading, margin trading, derivatives or a PoA (they can add these later). The Rights and Obligations, RDD, Guidance Note and identity/address proofs still apply, but only one proof of address is needed. PMLA/AML rules still apply.
FPIs submit a Common Application Form (CAF) and 'Annexure to CAF' (master circular of May 30, 2024); FPI registration was simplified on November 12, 2024.
SARAL is cash segment only, with no internet trading, margin trading, derivatives or PoA at the start.

sections.title: KYC, Digital KYC and In-Person Verification

blocks.text: KYC is the customer identification process: verifying identity, address, financial status, occupation and other prescribed details. All intermediaries use the same KYC form and documents, physically or digitally. KYC and Customer Due Diligence (CDD) are the base of anti-money laundering: collect and verify Proof of Identity and Proof of Address under the PMLA, 2002, PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 and SEBI's AML Master Circular of June 06, 2024.

items.title: Consent
items.text: Take the client's express consent.

items.title: Capture
items.text: PAN, name, photo, contacts captured digitally; signed by e-signature such as Aadhaar e-Sign.

items.title: Other documents

blocks.text: To use Aadhaar authentication, brokers act as KUAs/Sub-KUAs (KYC User Agencies) under Ministry of Finance guidelines: they register with UIDAI and sign an agreement with a KUA. After a Supreme Court judgement (April 30, 2025), digital KYC must be accessible to persons with disabilities; all digital platforms of regulated entities must comply with the RPwD Act, 2016.

In-Person Verification (IPV) is mandatory. The KYC form records the IPV person's name, designation, organisation, signature and date. IPV by one SEBI intermediary can be relied upon by another, and the broker's Authorised Persons may also do it.

Video IPV (VIPV) through the broker's app is allowed: done live by a trained official after informed consent; clear video, face uncovered; random questions with display of the officially valid document, KYC form and signature (or OTP); Aadhaar photo must match; recording stored tamper-proof with date and time stamp, plus activity log and official's credentials.

PAN is the sole identification number for the securities market, whatever the transaction amount. Brokers verify it online on the Income Tax website without insisting on the card. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, a PAN not linked to Aadhaar becomes inoperative; the KRA system flags linkage status.

blocks.text: Proof of Address/Identity: Passport, Aadhaar, Voter ID, Driving Licence, etc. If permanent and correspondence addresses differ, prove both. A third party's address can be the correspondence address only if that party's KYC is done (CDD as per Rule 9 of the PML Rules). The name on the KYC form must match the PoI. Identify any beneficial owner other than the client (AML Master Circular, June 06, 2024) and update CDD data periodically. Non-individuals give extra documents.

Mobile and e-mail go into the KRA system; never those of employees, APs or distributors. Bank: a cancelled cheque leaf plus bank statement/passbook copy; the account is mapped, and money is generally accepted only from mapped account(s) (more than one allowed, with proof), so that funds come only from the client himself. Demat: copy of the DP's client master; clients often give the broker a DDPI/PoA.

Running account authorisation: funds must be settled within 24 hours of pay-out unless the client authorises a running account. It must be signed by the client only, not a PoA holder, and the broker must still actually settle at least once a calendar quarter or month, as the client prefers.

Arjun's sale proceeds of ₹1,00,000 are paid out to the broker on Tuesday. With no running account authorisation, the broker must send the money to Arjun within 24 hours. If Arjun signs one and picks monthly settlement, the broker can hold the balance for his next trades but must settle at least once a month.

Risk Disclosure Document: risks of volatility, low liquidity, rumours, news, systems and options, plus features and risks of wireless/SOR trading; must be read before trading.
Nomination is voluntary (SEBI, September 26, 2023): nominate or opt out, but the account is activated only after the 'choice of nomination' is received in SEBI's format.

Financial proof is compulsory for derivatives clients (others as per the broker's RMS): ITR acknowledgement, annual accounts, salary slip/Form 16, net-worth certificate, bank statement for the last 6 months, demat holding statement, other asset proof, or self-declaration with support.
Brokers must keep all client information confidential, except where a law requires disclosure.
Running account letter: client signs, never a PoA holder; settle at least monthly or quarterly. Bank statement: 6 months.

sections.title: KRA and the Central KYC Records Registry (3.2.1.3-3.2.1.4)

blocks.text: In 2011 SEBI created the KYC Registration Agency (KRA) system to centralise securities-market KYC and avoid repeating it with every intermediary. Clients can trade once KYC is done, but those whose KYC attributes KRAs cannot verify cannot transact further until verified. KRAs show KYC status on their websites and must disseminate and display the Investor Charter.

The CKYCR (Central KYC Records Registry) is one KYC for the whole financial sector. The Government of India authorised CERSAI (set up under Section 20(1) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002) to act as CKYCR under the PML Rules, 2005. Since the 2015 amendment to the PML Rules, every reporting entity shares KYC with CKYCR in CERSAI's template.

Since 2001, brokers must allot every client a Unique Client Code (UCC) after KYC and use it on every order. The UCC is mapped to PAN and to the client's demat account. Why? So that every order on the exchange can be traced to one real, verified person, which stops trading in fictitious or borrowed names.

Each client needs a separate mobile and e-mail (never an employee's, remisier's or AP's), except, on specific written request, clients of one family or the authorised person of an HUF, company, firm or trust. Key KYC details must be kept updated.
The client gets a copy of all signed documents free, within 7 days, and acknowledges it. The trading code, UCC and e-mail ID for ECNs are communicated in writing.

Two trading codes: investors who by regulation cannot trade without funds/securities to their credit and settle delivery only may get up to two codes (buy and sell), so legs are not netted; both map to one UCC and STT is on a delivery basis.
UCC = the client's 'Aadhaar at the exchange': one per client, tied to PAN and demat, checked on every order.
Look-alike timelines: contract note 24 hours, copy of documents 7 days, CKYCR upload 10 days.
A PoA lets the broker (or broker-DP) operate the client's demat and bank accounts for deliveries and fund pay-in/pay-out (SEBI circulars of 2010 and August 27, 2020).
PoA is optional: it cannot be insisted on and services cannot be denied without it. Exception: internet based trading is exempted from this clause.

blocks.text: A PoA must name the BO and bank accounts covered and be in the name of the SEBI-registered entity, not an employee. Off-market transfers need a DIS signed by the client or an eDIS, with OTP consent.

DDPI (Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction), introduced in April 2022 to curb PoA misuse, can be used only for: (1) delivering securities for settlement of trades through the same broker; (2) pledging/re-pledging for margin to the TM/CM; (3) mutual fund transactions on exchange platforms; (4) tendering shares in open offers.

DDPI is optional: the client may use a physical DIS or eDIS instead, and cannot be compelled or denied service. Existing PoAs stay valid until revoked, but no new PoAs are executed for these purposes.

Order management = entering, modifying, cancelling and matching orders, during market hours only. An order has six components: price, time, quantity, security, action (buy/sell) and client identity (UCC/PAN). Conditions are of three kinds: price, time, quantity.

Market order: executes at the best available price(s) across market depth; no price is given. Market with protection combines market and limit: it executes only up to a level the trader sets, so it can't fill at any price. A limit order sets the price (buy at or below, sell at or above); it may never fill. Unmatched orders resting in the book are passive; incoming ones are active; trades happen at the passive price.

Best sell: 100 @ ₹807.60, then 119 @ ₹807.75. A market buy of 100 trades 100 @ ₹807.60. A limit buy of 200 @ ₹807.60 trades 100 @ ₹807.60 and the other 100 waits in the book as the new best buy at ₹807.60.

blocks.text: Market order = certainty of execution, not price. Limit order = certainty of price, not execution. Market with protection = a market order wearing a seat belt.

Stop loss order: enters the market only when price reaches or crosses the trigger price; the client gives a trigger plus a limit (or market) price. A trader who bought at ₹100 and will risk only ₹5 places a sell stop loss, trigger ₹96, limit ₹95.

sections.title: Order Modification, Trade Execution and Trade Annulment (3.2.3-3.2.4)

blocks.text: Orders can be modified until fully executed and cancelled in market hours to the extent not executed. Once matched, the exchange notifies the broker, who tells the client immediately or at day end; the official communication is the contract note. After execution only the client code and CP code can be modified.

items: Client code changes for non-institutional trades only to fix a genuine entry error; the exchange runs a special inspection.

Moving a trade to the broker's error account isn't a modification if it is later liquidated in the market. Error account codes are disclosed to exchanges; a management-approved error policy is required.
Penalties go to the exchange's Investor Protection Fund; waivable for a proven genuine error.
Pro trades can never become client trades, or vice versa.
Institutional: between schemes/sub-accounts of the same institution allowed, no penalty; between unrelated institutions, penalty.
CP code can be modified on the trade day within exchange/CC timings.

head: Trade annulment (SEBI, July 16, 2015)
Rule
rows: 5% of trade value, min ₹1 lakh, max ₹10 lakh (exchange may raise the cap)
Exchange can examine trades on its own

blocks.text: Trade of ₹10 lakh: 5% = ₹50,000, so the fee is the floor, ₹1 lakh. Trade of ₹5 crore: 5% = ₹25 lakh, so the fee is capped at ₹10 lakh.
blocks.title: Annulment fee

blocks.text: Annulment fees and client code penalties go to the exchange's Investor Protection Fund, not SEBI. And the workbook's 3.2.3 says orders 'not fully or partially executed' can be cancelled; read with 3.2.2.2, the unexecuted part of a partly filled order can still be cancelled.

The middle office sits between front and back: validations, bookings, confirmations, and above all risk management and surveillance. The reason: the obligation to settle lies with the broker, so if a client defaults the broker pays the clearing corporation.

Margin is what the CC levies on the broker for positions, in proportion to exposure. The broker collects it upfront from clients, allows trading against their collateral, checks risk as each order arrives, and sets exposure and turnover limits per client. SEBI/exchanges set requirements by broker type (exchange terminals, CTCL, IBT, STWT, SOR, algo). Firm-level procedures:

items: Standards and reports
Position limits
Investment guidelines and strategies
Systems to report compliance with policies
Assessing effectiveness of strategies, policies, procedures

blocks.text: A client buys shares worth ₹5 lakh on Monday and then doesn't pay. On T+1 the clearing corporation still expects ₹5 lakh from the broker, and the broker must pay it from its own pocket. That is why the RMS asks for upfront margin and enforces client limits before the order ever reaches the exchange.
blocks.title: Why the broker cares

blocks.text: The broker is the guarantor; the middle office is the bouncer checking every order at the door.

head: Risk
Meaning and broker examples
rows: Loss from failed internal processes, manual/system errors or external events: handling client assets, non-compliance, trading errors, non-payment/non-delivery, client denying a matched order, sudden bank closure, unauthorised trading, fraud, poor books, inexperienced staff, unstable or easily accessed systems

Loss from adverse price moves: concentration of client collateral in stocks/sectors, broker's own investments; driven by fiscal gap, debt, terrorism, energy shocks, interest rates; includes cost of borrowing securities, dividend and correlation risk

Default by a borrower: loans to group companies, client debit balances, client funding, short margin collection, non-confirmation of DVP trade by custodian; reduced by collateral, margin payments and netting clauses
Contract can't be enforced: illegal, or the other party lacked authority
'Domino effect' of failures, or a 'crisis of confidence' making markets illiquid

blocks.text: Risk management should begin at the point nearest to where risk is assumed: trade entry, client documentation, client engagement, limits.
Systemic risk = dominoes: one firm falls, knocks over the next, and soon nobody trusts anybody.
Custodian not confirming a DVP trade and short margin = credit; client denying a matched order = operational; concentrated client collateral = market.

Rumours: staff must not circulate unverified news; social media/messaging use is supervised with logs kept as records; market news can be forwarded only with the Compliance Officer's approval, or both employee and officer face SEBI action. Violations of the Code of Conduct under the SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 must be reported to exchanges.

Chapter IV of the SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations, 2026 (institutional mechanism against fraud and market abuse) requires: surveillance systems and internal controls, documented policies, fraud prevention/detection duties, escalation and reporting, and a whistle blower policy. Members also need a Surveillance Policy, client monitoring and mandatory warnings on trading software (PMLA).
Reversal trades (non-genuine trades to shift profit/loss or fake volume) are cancelled by the exchanges' Reversal Trade Cancellation Mechanism (RTCM), which works intraday.
Forwarding market news? Only with the Compliance Officer's approval, or both the employee and the officer face SEBI action.

blocks.text: The back office handles post-market processing: confirmation, payments, settlements and accounting. It is where the trade ends.

Trade enrichment adds further information to an already executed trade, automatically after each trade: whatever is needed to clear F&O or settle cash trades. Back-office masters (client-wise brokerage rates, GST, stamp duty, STT tables) are appended to each trade to compute client-wise brokerage, client-wise fund/securities obligations and taxes, and to produce exchange obligations, contract notes and settlement and tax figures.

Trade allocation: for institutions, the front office may place one order under CP code 'INST' and the back office splits it across the client's schemes (pro rata, all or nothing, etc.), as a hedge fund does across its portfolios.

sections.title: Accounting: Books, Records and How Long to Keep Them

blocks.text: Books are kept under Rule 15 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957 and Regulation 15 of the SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations, 2026 (electronic records must meet the IT Act, 2000). Keep separate books per exchange, separate client ledgers per segment, and client-wise books. Under CC interoperability, ledgers may be segment-wise and consolidated across exchanges, but the exchange-wise break-up must be shown in inspections.

blocks.text: Regulation 16: preserve books and records for at least eight years.

Books must separate (a) money from or for each client from (b) the member's own money, with chronological client-wise records of money and securities received and delivered. Client collateral may be used only for that client's margin/pay-in, with an audit trail.
8 years for books vs 3 years for order evidence. Books are under the SC(R) Rules, 1957, not the SC(R) Act, 1956.

Brokers need one integrated system for back office, real-time order execution and risk, with archiving, audit trail, DR protocols and standby databases. Software needs UAT and mock trading, with reports certified by independent system auditors before release. Brokers should consider software escrow; large brokers, multiple vendors; and staff must be trained.

System audits are periodic, by broker category (exchange system, CTCL/DMA, algo), covering controls, RMS, passwords, network, access, backup, database security and change management. SEBI's January 31, 2025 circular added technology-based monitoring of these audits.
Brokers must not outsource core business and compliance functions, e.g. order execution and monitoring of clients' trading.

BCP/DR: a written plan for significant disruptions is desirable for all; it is mandatory for brokers above the minimum client base specified by exchanges. It must let the broker meet its obligations to customers and cover its relationships with other broker-dealers and counterparties. They need a BCP-DR policy with SOPs, health monitoring of critical systems, and periodic review.
BCP/DR is mandatory only above the exchange-specified minimum client base (desirable for all). Order execution and monitoring of client trading are core and cannot be outsourced.

sections.title: Handling Technical Glitches and Exchange Outages

blocks.text: IRRA discontinued. By circular dated March 27, 2026, SEBI discontinued the Investor Risk Reduction Access (IRRA) platform, because exchanges now offer an alternative: the Contingency Pool Trading facility. It lets brokers square off clients' outstanding open positions during business disruptions, over the exchange's internal network within its premises, using dedicated terminals allocated by the broker and connected to the exchange trading platform.

items.title: Before: IRRA platform
points: Let clients of a broker hit by an outage reduce risk on open positions

items.title: Now: Contingency Pool Trading
points: Broker squares off clients' open positions during disruptions
Inside the exchange premises, on its internal network, via dedicated terminals

blocks.text: Interoperable segments: NSE and BSE act as backup venues for each other. Common products can be offset on the working exchange; for exclusive scrips, exchanges create reserve contracts or correlated products. The affected exchange informs SEBI and the other exchange within 75 minutes; the backup activates its BCP within 15 minutes of that. SEBI's January 09, 2023 SOP covers outage definition, reporting, trading on unaffected venues, extension of trading hours and BCP updates.

Technical glitch: any malfunction (hardware, software, network, process; own or outsourced) in a broker's trading/risk systems during market hours that stops, slows or varies log-in, order handling or margin/fund viewing for five minutes or more continuously. The framework covers brokers offering IBT/STWT with more than 10,000 registered clients (excluding closed accounts) as on 31 March of the previous financial year. SEBI lists some issues that are not glitches, and glitches that don't affect service to clients attract no financial disincentive.

blocks.text: Brokers must plan capacity for growing clients and monitor systems through the API-based Logging and Monitoring Mechanism (LAMA) with exchanges.

A broker with 2 lakh app clients sees its order screen freeze from 10:00 to 10:12 am on Monday. Twelve minutes is over the 5-minute mark, so it is a technical glitch. The broker must inform the exchanges and clients by 12:00 noon, file the Preliminary Incident Report by Tuesday (T+1) and the RCA within 14 days.

IRRA is gone; for broker outages the answer now is the exchanges' Contingency Pool Trading facility. Don't mix the glitch framework's 10,000 clients with CSCRF client thresholds.

SEBI's CSCRF (circular of August 20, 2024, effective in phases from January 1, 2025) applies to brokers, depositories and other regulated entities (REs) and supersedes earlier cyber guidelines. Cyber resilience = ability to anticipate, withstand and recover from attacks.

A Security Operation Centre (SOC) is required (own, group-level or third-party). For smaller entities, NSE and BSE must run Market SOCs (M-SOC). The framework stresses 'informed preparedness' (spotting attacks early), 'localisation' (isolating a crisis so trusted functions continue) and 'Evolve' (upgrading defences as threats change). Compliance is non-negotiable.
CSCRF takes a graded approach, sorting REs into five categories by clients, trading volume, AUM, etc.: MIIs, Qualified, Mid-size, Small-size and Self-certification REs.
Exempt: brokers with under ₹1,000 crore yearly client volume and under 1,000 clients. All members need an SOP for cyber incidents.

A broker has 50,000 registered clients whose trading volume is ₹40,000 crore a year. Both fall in the 'more than 10,000 up to 1 lakh' and 'more than ₹10,000 crore up to ₹1,00,000 crore' bands, so it is a Small-size RE. A broker with 800 clients and ₹600 crore volume is exempt.

blocks.text: Goals as a boxer: see it coming, take the hit, limit damage, get up, get better.
Detection/Protection are functions; Contain/Evolve are goals. M-SOCs are run by NSE and BSE.

flashcards.q: Which office handles risk management in a broking firm?
flashcards.a: The middle office (along with surveillance).

flashcards.q: Which trade life cycle steps are back office functions?
flashcards.a: Confirmation of trades, and clearing and settlement.

flashcards.q: What is co-location?
flashcards.a: Exchange lets brokers/data vendors place systems in or near its premises, linked to the trading platform by a direct private network.

flashcards.q: Name the six acceptable forms of order-placing evidence.
flashcards.a: Signed physical record, telephone recording, e-mail from authorised ID, internet log, SMS record, any other legally verifiable record.

flashcards.q: What is DMA?
flashcards.a: Direct Market Access: clients reach the exchange through the broker's infrastructure without manual broker intervention. Introduced 2008 for institutions.

flashcards.q: Define algorithmic trading.
flashcards.a: Any order generated using automated execution logic.

flashcards.q: What marks out High Frequency Trading?
flashcards.a: Latency-sensitive algo trading with high daily portfolio turnover and high order-to-trade ratio (OTR).

flashcards.q: In retail API algo trading, who is principal and who is agent?
flashcards.a: The broker is the principal; the algo provider/fintech is the broker's agent.

flashcards.q: What is STP?
flashcards.a: Straight Through Processing: one-pass electronic processing from deal to settlement; mandatory for institutional trades since 2004.

flashcards.q: Who confirms an institutional trade, and how is it routed to them?
flashcards.a: The custodian (a clearing member), via the CP code entered at order entry.

flashcards.q: What is a contract note?
flashcards.a: The legal record and confirmation of a day's trades, creating a legally enforceable broker-client relationship. Issued within 24 hours.

flashcards.q: ECN bounced. What now?
flashcards.a: Keep a bounce mail log and send a physical contract note within the stipulated time, with proof of delivery.

flashcards.q: Statutory charges vs regulatory levies on a contract note?
flashcards.a: Statutory: STT, GST, stamp duty. Regulatory: SEBI turnover fees, exchange transaction charges.

flashcards.q: What are the two parts of the Account Opening Form?
flashcards.a: Part I: KYC form (CERSAI template). Part II: additional trading-account information.

flashcards.q: Who can use SARAL AOF?
flashcards.a: New individual investors in the cash segment not using internet trading, margin trading, derivatives or PoA.

flashcards.q: When is IPV not required?
flashcards.a: When KYC is done via Aadhaar authentication of UIDAI, or submitted online with documents via DigiLocker/online-verifiable source.

flashcards.q: Who may perform IPV for a broker?
flashcards.a: The broker's staff or its Authorised Persons; IPV by another SEBI intermediary can also be relied upon.

flashcards.q: Who is exempt from mandatory PAN?
flashcards.a: Central/State Government and court-appointed officials, Sikkim residents, and tax-exempt UN/multilateral agencies.

flashcards.q: Who signs a running account authorisation?
flashcards.a: Only the client, never a PoA holder. Settlement still at least quarterly or monthly.

flashcards.q: What is a KRA?
flashcards.a: KYC Registration Agency: SEBI's 2011 system centralising securities-market KYC records.

flashcards.q: Who acts as the Central KYC Records Registry?
flashcards.a: CERSAI, authorised by the Government of India; brokers upload KYC within 10 days.

flashcards.q: What is mapped to the UCC?
flashcards.a: The client's PAN and demat account; exchanges validate UCC and PAN on every order.

flashcards.q: When can one mobile number be uploaded for several clients?
flashcards.a: On specific written request: members of one family, or the authorised person of an HUF, company, firm or trust.

flashcards.q: Why allot two trading codes to a client?
flashcards.a: For delivery-only investors, so buy and sell legs aren't netted; both map to one UCC.

flashcards.q: Is PoA compulsory?
flashcards.a: No. Services can't be denied without it; only internet based trading is exempted from this clause.

flashcards.q: What are DDPI's four permitted uses?
flashcards.a: Settlement deliveries via same broker, margin pledge to TM/CM, MF transactions on exchange, tendering in open offers.

flashcards.q: Maximum brokerage on options?
flashcards.a: 2.5% of premium or ₹100 per lot, whichever is higher; charged on premium, not strike.

flashcards.q: What is a market with protection order?
flashcards.a: A market order that executes only up to a price level set by the trader.

flashcards.q: Passive vs active order?
flashcards.a: Passive: resting unmatched in the book. Active: incoming order that matches. Trades happen at the passive price.

flashcards.q: What does IOC mean?
flashcards.a: Immediate or Cancel: matches on release; any unmatched part is cancelled immediately. Partial fills allowed.

flashcards.q: What is a Disclosed Quantity order?
flashcards.a: Shows only part of the order to the market, releasing the next part as each is traded.

flashcards.q: Which order conditions are currently unavailable?
flashcards.a: GTC, GTD, AON and MF, as per SEBI directives.

flashcards.q: Call auction: how is the equilibrium price chosen?
flashcards.a: Maximum tradable quantity; then minimum unmatched quantity; then closest to reference price.

flashcards.q: Can a pro trade be modified into a client trade?
flashcards.a: Never, and vice versa.

flashcards.q: Trade annulment: window and fee?
flashcards.a: Within 30 minutes (60 in exceptional cases); fee 5% of trade value, ₹1 lakh to ₹10 lakh, to the IPF.

flashcards.q: What is operational risk?
flashcards.a: Loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, manual/system errors or external events.

flashcards.q: What is systemic risk?
flashcards.a: A domino effect of failures across markets, or a crisis of confidence causing illiquidity.

flashcards.q: What is RTCM?
flashcards.a: Reversal Trade Cancellation Mechanism: exchanges cancel reversal trades on an intraday basis.

flashcards.q: What is trade enrichment?
flashcards.a: Automatically adding clearing/settlement details, brokerage and taxes to each executed trade.

flashcards.q: What does CP code 'INST' signal?
flashcards.a: A single institutional order to be allocated across the client's schemes at the back office.

flashcards.q: What is the sauda book?
flashcards.a: The register of transactions: every trade with security, value, rates and client.

flashcards.q: What replaced the IRRA platform in 2026?
flashcards.a: Stock exchanges' Contingency Pool Trading facility, to square off clients' open positions during disruptions.

flashcards.q: What is LAMA?
flashcards.a: API-based Logging and Monitoring Mechanism between exchanges and brokers' trading systems.

flashcards.q: CSCRF's five resiliency goals?
flashcards.a: Anticipate, Withstand, Contain, Recover, Evolve.

flashcards.q: Who runs Market SOCs?
flashcards.a: NSE and BSE, for smaller regulated entities.

flashcards.q: Bulk deal vs block deal?
flashcards.a: Bulk: over 0.5% of listed shares in the normal market. Block: single trade of at least ₹25 crore in a separate window.

flashcards.q: Who keeps corporate benefits in SLB?
flashcards.a: The lender, the actual owner of the securities.

flashcards.q: Stamp duty on securities is shared on what basis?
flashcards.a: The state of domicile of the buyer.

questions.q: SEBI introduced the Direct Market Access (DMA) facility mainly for:
questions.why: SEBI introduced DMA in 2008 and permitted institutional investors to use it.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: On receiving an order, the exchange sends an order confirmation to the broker
Depending on its terms and market prices, an order may execute immediately, partially or fully
The exchange time-stamps every order it receives
An order can be entered for a client irrespective of whether he has sufficient funds or securities
questions.why: The broker's RMS lets through only orders within limits and backed by sufficient upfront margin.

questions.q: A contract note is best described as:
options: A legal agreement the client signs with the broker before any transaction
A note holding the client's margin details
Confirmation of trades done on a particular day, with securities, prices and other details
The client registration form uploaded to the exchange
questions.why: A contract note confirms the trades done on a day for the client and is the legal record of those transactions.

questions.q: Maintenance of different books of account by stock brokers is prescribed under:
questions.why: Rule 15 of the SC(R) Rules, 1957 (with Regulation 15 of the SEBI Stock Brokers Regulations) prescribes the books.

questions.q: A broker must obtain prior approval for every advertisement from:
questions.why: Members must obtain prior approval from the exchange and follow its Code for Advertisements.

questions.q: The SEBI turnover fee for the interest rate derivatives segment is:
questions.why: IRD attracts ₹5 per crore; equity and currency derivatives ₹10; debt ₹2.

questions.q: Market making is mandatory for an initial period of 3 years in the:
questions.why: Market making is mandatory for 3 years for SME securities.

questions.q: The regular pre-open session in the equity segment starts at:
questions.why: Pre-open runs 9:00-9:15 am; 8:45 is the morning block window and 9:15 the normal market.

questions.q: The Investor Risk Reduction Access (IRRA) platform, discontinued by SEBI in March 2026, was provided by:
questions.why: IRRA was an exchange platform; SEBI discontinued it because exchanges now offer an alternative, the Contingency Pool Trading facility.

questions.q: Which of these is a statutory levy?
questions.why: STT (with GST and stamp duty) is statutory; SEBI fees and exchange charges are regulatory levies.

questions.q: After SEBI's circular of March 27, 2026, what lets a broker square off clients' outstanding open positions during a business disruption?
options: The stock exchanges' Contingency Pool Trading facility
questions.why: SEBI discontinued IRRA because exchanges provide the Contingency Pool Trading facility for exactly this.

questions.q: The exchanges' Contingency Pool Trading facility operates:
options: Over the internet from the broker's disaster recovery site
Via the exchange's internal network within its premises, on dedicated terminals allocated by the broker
Through the Market SOC run by NSE and BSE
questions.why: It runs on the exchange's internal network inside its physical premises, with broker-allocated dedicated terminals.

questions.q: A contract note must be issued to the client within:
questions.why: The contract note is issued within 24 hours of execution of the contract.

questions.q: An electronic contract note e-mailed to a client bounces. The broker must:
options: Do nothing, as the ECN is also on its website
Send a physical contract note within the stipulated time and keep proof of delivery
questions.why: Where ECNs are not delivered or bounce, the broker sends a physical copy within the stipulated time and maintains proof of delivery.

questions.q: In the normal case, how long must a broker keep evidence of a client's order placement?
questions.why: Records are kept for the period arbitration accepts complaints, currently three years (longer if a dispute is pending).

questions.q: Under Regulation 16 of the SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations, 2026, books and records must be preserved for at least:
questions.why: Books and records under Regulation 15 are preserved for a minimum of eight years.

questions.q: A broker must upload a new client's KYC records to the CKYCR within:
questions.why: Stock brokers file the KYC with CKYCR within 10 days after commencement of an account-based relationship.

questions.q: A copy of all documents executed by the client must be given to him:
options: On payment of a fee, within 30 days
Only if he asks for it
questions.why: Copies are given free of charge within 7 days from execution, with the client's acknowledgement.

questions.q: Which statement about running account authorisation is correct?
options: It must be signed by the client, and the account settled at least once a calendar quarter or month as he prefers
It may be signed by the client's PoA holder
Once given, the broker need never settle the account
It requires settlement only once a year
questions.why: Authorisation is signed by the client only, and actual settlement happens at least quarterly or monthly per the client's preference.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT exempt from the mandatory PAN requirement?
options: An Official Liquidator appointed by a court
UN entities exempt from Indian tax
questions.why: Exemptions cover government/court officials, Sikkim residents and tax-exempt UN/multilateral bodies. NRIs are not exempt.

questions.q: In-Person Verification is NOT required when:
options: The client is a senior citizen
KYC is completed using Aadhaar authentication of UIDAI
The client trades only in the cash segment
The client opts for physical contract notes
questions.why: IPV is not needed where KYC uses UIDAI Aadhaar authentication, or online KYC with DigiLocker documents.

questions.q: SARAL AOF can be used by a new individual investor who:
options: Trades only in the cash segment without internet trading, margin, derivatives or PoA
questions.why: SARAL is for new individuals in the cash segment not availing internet trading, margin trading, derivatives or PoA.

questions.q: For investors who must settle on a delivery-only basis, a broker may allot up to two trading codes. These codes are:
options: Mapped to the same UCC, so buy and sell legs are not netted
questions.why: Both codes map to the same UCC; keeping buys and sells separate prevents netting, and STT is on a delivery basis.

questions.q: Statement: With the introduction of DDPI, all existing Powers of Attorney given by clients stood automatically cancelled.
questions.why: False. Existing PoAs remain valid until the client revokes them; new PoAs are no longer executed for DDPI purposes.

questions.q: Statement: Stock exchanges validate UCC and PAN at order entry for both PRO and CLI orders.
questions.why: True. Exchanges validate UCC and PAN for all orders in all markets, PRO and CLI.

questions.q: A client buys 1 lot (75 units) of an option at a premium of ₹40. The maximum brokerage the broker may charge is:
questions.why: Premium value ₹3,000 x 2.5% = ₹75; ₹100 per lot is higher, and the rule is whichever is higher.

questions.q: For a share priced at ₹8, the maximum brokerage per share is:
options: There is no limit for low-priced shares
questions.why: If the share value is ₹10 or less, a maximum of 25 paise per share can be collected.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT decide priority in continuous order matching?
questions.why: Matching is on price-time priority; quantity is not a factor.

questions.q: The best sell order is 100 shares @ ₹807.60 (next 119 @ ₹807.75). A limit buy order for 200 @ ₹807.65 arrives. What happens?
options: 100 trade at ₹807.60 and 100 rest in the book as the best buy at ₹807.65
questions.why: Trades happen at the passive order's price (₹807.60); the unmatched balance waits as the best buy.

questions.q: A client who bought at ₹830 places a sell stop loss with trigger ₹800 and limit ₹790. When the price falls to ₹800:
options: A sell order at ₹790 enters the market and matches only with a buy at ₹790 or better
The shares are sold at exactly ₹800
The shares are sold at any available price
A buy order at ₹790 is placed
questions.why: Once triggered, an SL-limit sell goes in at the limit price and matches only at that price or better.

questions.q: Which of these order conditions can be used today?
questions.why: GTC, GTD, AON and MF are currently not available as per SEBI directives; IOC is.

questions.q: Statement: An IOC order can be partly executed, with the unmatched portion cancelled immediately.
questions.why: True. Partial match is possible for IOC; the rest is cancelled at once.

questions.q: In a call auction, two prices both give the maximum tradable quantity. The equilibrium price is the one with:
questions.why: The tie-breaker after maximum quantity is minimum unmatched quantity, then closeness to the reference price.

questions.q: In a call auction, cumulative demand/supply are: ₹104: 37,000/21,300; ₹105: 27,500/36,300; ₹106: 15,500/48,300. The equilibrium price is:
questions.why: Tradable quantity is the lower of demand and supply: 21,300, 27,500, 15,500. The maximum, 27,500, is at ₹105.

questions.q: A broker of one exchange wants to deal with a broker of another exchange for proprietary trading. It may do so:
options: With any number of brokers, after SEBI approval
With only one such broker, after intimating its parent exchange
questions.why: A broker can deal with only one broker of another exchange for proprietary trading, after intimating the parent exchange.

questions.q: A trade annulment request is normally to be made within:
options: 30 minutes of the trade (up to 60 in exceptional cases)
The end of the trading day
questions.why: Requests are made within 30 minutes; exchanges may consider up to 60 minutes in exceptional cases.

questions.q: A broker seeks annulment of a ₹10 lakh trade. The application fee is:
questions.why: 5% of ₹10 lakh is ₹50,000, below the minimum, so the minimum fee of ₹1 lakh applies.

questions.q: Which trade modification is NEVER allowed?
options: Correcting a genuine client-code entry error in a non-institutional trade
Moving a trade between two schemes of the same mutual fund
Changing a proprietary trade into a client trade
Modifying the CP code on trade day within permitted time
questions.why: Proprietary trades can't be modified as client trades and vice versa.

questions.q: For a broker, 'non-confirmation of a DVP trade by the custodian' is an example of:
questions.why: The workbook lists it, with client debit balances and short margin collection, under credit risk.

questions.q: Under the technical glitch framework, a malfunction counts as a 'technical glitch' if it lasts for a contiguous period of:
questions.why: A glitch is a stoppage, slowdown or variance for a contiguous period of five minutes or more.

questions.q: After a technical glitch, the Root Cause Analysis report must reach the exchange within:
questions.why: Inform within 2 hours, preliminary report within T+1, RCA within 14 days.

questions.q: If one exchange suffers an outage, it must inform SEBI and the alternate exchange within:
questions.why: The affected exchange informs within 75 minutes; the alternate venue activates BCP within 15 minutes of intimation.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of CSCRF's five cyber resiliency goals?
questions.why: Goals: Anticipate, Withstand, Contain, Recover, Evolve. Detection is one of the six core functions.

questions.q: A broker has 50,000 registered clients and ₹40,000 crore yearly clientele trading volume. Under CSCRF it is a:
questions.why: Clients above 10,000 up to 1 lakh and volume above ₹10,000 up to ₹1,00,000 crore fall in Small-size.

questions.q: STT on an equity option that is exercised is:
options: 0.1% on premium, paid by the seller
0.125% on intrinsic value, paid by the buyer
0.02% on contract value, paid by the seller
0.025% on intrinsic value, paid by the buyer
questions.why: Exercised options attract 0.125% on intrinsic value, payable by the buyer of the option.

questions.q: A broker must disclose a bulk deal when the quantity traded in a scrip exceeds:
options: 0.5% of the company's listed equity shares
questions.why: Bulk deal disclosure applies above 0.5% of the number of listed equity shares; ₹25 crore is the block deal minimum.

questions.q: The reference price for the afternoon block deal window is:
options: The opening price of the day
The VWAP of trades in the cash segment between 1:45 pm and 2:00 pm
The VWAP of the whole trading day
questions.why: Afternoon window (2:05-2:20 pm) uses VWAP of 1:45-2:00 pm; the morning window uses the previous close.

questions.q: Which describes the post-close session?
options: 3:40-4:00 pm, only market orders, at the closing price
3:40-4:00 pm, both limit and market orders
questions.why: Post-close runs 3:40-4:00 pm; only market orders are allowed, with single price matching at the close price.

questions.q: In an Offer for Sale through the stock exchange, if an investor defaults on pay-in, the penalty is:
options: Recovered from the Settlement Guarantee Fund
questions.why: Default attracts a 10% penalty on order value; the SGF is not available for OFS.

questions.q: Under the Securities Lending and Borrowing Scheme, corporate benefits on lent shares go to the:
questions.why: Corporate actions and benefits remain with the lender, the actual owner.
